objective: By the end of this lesson you can do an instrument-pilot postflight inspection, write up any discrepancies and servicing needs so maintenance can act on them, and explain what may and may not be deferred under 14 CFR 91.213, who must sign which entries, and how the VOR check is logged.
why: Instruments that misbehave in the clouds are often still working fine on the ramp. If you don't record what you saw, the next pilot may launch into IMC with the same problem and no warning.

prereading.what: Engine shutdown, post-flight inspection, securing and servicing.
prereading.label: AFH 2-23

prereading.what: Inspections, operations with inoperative equipment, MELs, preventive maintenance and maintenance entries.
prereading.label: PHAK 9-8 to 9-10

prereading.what: Operating without an MEL: removal, deactivation, placarding, continued operation and safety risk analysis.
prereading.label: AC 91-67A, 4-1 to 4-3

prereading.what: VOR accuracy, VOR receiver checks, VOT and certified checkpoints.
prereading.label: IFH 9-16 to 9-17

prereading.what: Additional reports to ATC, including loss of navigation or communication capability.
prereading.label: AIM 5-3-3

prereading.what: Identifying hazards, including postflight inspections and inoperative equipment as aircraft hazards.
prereading.label: RMH 3-4 to 3-7

warmup: On today's IFR flight the attitude indicator drifted a few degrees in a long turn, then seemed fine. After landing it looks normal. What would the next pilot need to know, and where would they look for it?

key_terms.def: Anything on the airplane that failed, acted abnormally or was found damaged. You record it so maintenance can fix it.
The maintenance record or squawk sheet provided for pilots to write up problems.
FAA-approved list, with a letter of authorization, of items that may be inoperative for a specific aircraft and the conditions for flying that way.
Flying a small non-turbine airplane without an MEL with an inoperative item that is not required, removed or deactivated, placarded, and found not to be a hazard.
List in the POH/AFM of equipment required for each kind of operation, such as VFR, IFR, day or night.
A legible marking next to the control or indicator of an inoperative item, telling the crew and mechanics its condition.
The signed maintenance record entry by an authorized person that says work was done right and the airplane may fly again.
Simple or minor preservation work and small standard part replacement listed in 14 CFR part 43 appendix A(c).
VOR test facility: a ground test signal used to check VOR receiver accuracy.
FAA permit that lets an airplane that doesn't meet airworthiness requirements, but can fly safely, be flown to a place for repair.

chunks.title: The flight is not over at shutdown

body.p: A flight is not complete until the engine is shut down and the airplane is secured [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. For an instrument pilot, there is one more job: tell maintenance and the next pilot about anything that went wrong.

head: Who
Responsibility
rows: You, the PIC
Decide whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight, and stop the flight if unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural problems occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]
Owner or operator
Primarily responsible for keeping the airplane airworthy [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]], and must have discrepancies repaired between required inspections [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]]
Mechanic or repair station
Does the maintenance and signs the record entries that return the airplane to service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(b)]]

body.p: The owner can't fix what nobody reported. Your write-up is the link between what you saw in the clouds and what the mechanic checks on the ground.

callout.text: The RMH lists postflight inspections as a way to find aircraft hazards before the next person flies. Typical finds: tires and brakes, loose access panels and latches, and leaking fluids [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

check.q: Who is primarily responsible for keeping the airplane airworthy, and who decides if it is safe for this flight?
check.a: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for airworthiness [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. The PIC decides whether it is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

chunks.title: Noticing and noting discrepancies in flight

body.p: You can only write up what you noticed. Know what normal looks like for each instrument and its power source. Before any flight by instrument reference, check all instruments and their sources of power [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

head: Normal (IFH checks)
Worth writing up if you saw it
rows: Suction (or electrical source) right for that airplane's gyros [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Suction low or out of range; gyros slow, noisy or drifting
Gyros spin up with no hesitation or unusual noise [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Hesitation, whining or grinding at start-up or shutdown
Altimeter within 75 ft of field elevation with the current setting [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Error of more than 75 ft. The IFH says refer it to a repair station
Compass bowl full of fluid, card moves freely, correction card in place [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Bubble in the bowl, sticky card, missing card
Pitot heat shows a load on the ammeter when turned on [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
No ammeter change, or airspeed lost in visible moisture

body.p: The vacuum pump drives the heading and attitude indicators, and the suction gauge shows the low pressure inside the instruments [[23:112|IFH 5-17]]. A low suction reading is an early clue to a failing gyro system.

Write down details while they are fresh. The AIM asks for these in a NAVAID or GPS anomaly report: date and time, NAVAID or GPS, where it started and ended, heading and altitude, avionics in use, what happened and for how long, the effect, and what you did about it [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]].

callout.text: In flight, use the AFM/POH procedures for a failure. Maintenance deferrals are not used for inflight discrepancies [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Deferral is a ground decision made before the next takeoff.
Check before you blame the VOR. Some propeller rpm settings make the CDI swing as much as ±6°. A small rpm change usually smooths it out [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

check.q: With the current altimeter setting, the altimeter reads 90 ft off field elevation. Is that a discrepancy?
check.a: Yes. More than 75 ft makes its accuracy questionable; refer it to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

body.p: Under IFR in controlled airspace, the PIC must report as soon as practical to ATC any malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment that occurs in flight [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]].

callout.text: The report must include: (1) aircraft identification, (2) equipment affected, (3) how much your ability to operate IFR in the ATC system is impaired, and (4) the nature and extent of help you want from ATC [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]].

head: Report to ATC (AIM 5-3-3)
Examples
rows: Loss of navigation receivers
VOR, TACAN, ADF or low frequency receiver capability [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]
GPS
GPS anomalies while using installed IFR-certified GPS/GNSS [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]
ILS
Complete or partial loss of ILS receiver capability [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]
Communications
Impairment of air/ground communications [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]
Other equipment
Anything, such as weather radar, that in your judgment affects safety or IFR capability [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]

body.p: Make the first report by radio to the controlling ATC facility or FSS, or by telephone to the ATC facility for that airspace. GPS problems should also be reported after the flight on the FAA GPS Anomaly Reporting Form [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]].
The ATC report does not replace the write-up. ATC helps you finish this flight. The discrepancy record protects the next one.

check.q: Under IFR in controlled airspace your #2 nav radio fails. What four things go in your report?
check.a: Aircraft ID, equipment affected, how much your IFR capability is impaired, and the help you want from ATC [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the postflight inspection

body.p: **After shutdown.** Use the AFM/POH shutdown checklist, including the magneto grounding check at idle [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. After the engine stops and passengers are out, do the walkaround [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

bullets: 1. Cowling: oil or fuel streaks, and excess oil at the breather [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
2. Under the wings and other tank areas: fuel stains [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
3. Landing gear and tires: damage. Brakes: leaking hydraulic fluid [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
4. Cowling inlets: obstructions [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
5. IFR items: condition of all antennas, pitot tube and static ports free of dirt and obstructions [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].
6. Anti-ice or deice fluid quantity, if equipped, so the next pilot knows what is available [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

body.p: **Servicing.** Check oil and bring it to the AFM/POH level. Add fuel based on the next use. If the airplane will sit, filling the tanks helps prevent water condensation [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
**Secure it.** Hangar or tie down, secure the flight controls, and install locks. Pitot tube covers and cowling inlet covers add protection [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
**Document.** Write up every discrepancy from the flight and the walkaround, and any servicing done or still needed, in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

callout.text: Write squawks a mechanic can act on: what, when, how long, and conditions. Example: 'Attitude indicator precessed about 5° right in prolonged left turns in IMC, 6,000 ft, suction in the green. Normal on ground.'

check.q: Name two IFR-specific items to add to the AFH postflight walkaround.
check.a: Antenna condition and pitot tube and static ports free of obstructions; also deice fluid quantity if equipped [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

chunks.title: Writing it up: records, signatures and who may do what

body.p: As the pilot, you make an entry in the maintenance record or the discrepancy record provided for that purpose [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Then the people who fix it make their own entries.

head: Entry
Who makes it
What it contains
rows: Maintenance or preventive maintenance (43.9)
The person who did the work
Description of work, date completed, name of the person who did it, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving it [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]
Inspection (43.11)
The person approving or disapproving return to service after a part 91 inspection
Type and extent of inspection, date, total time in service, signature, certificate number and kind [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)]]
Discrepancy list at an inspection (43.11(b))
The inspector
Signed, dated list to the owner; each item allowed inoperative under 91.213(d)(2) placarded 'Inoperative' [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]]

body.p: No one may approve the airplane for return to service until the 43.9 or 43.11 entry is made [[60:131|14 CFR 43.5(a)]]. And no one may operate it after maintenance until it is approved for return to service and that entry exists [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

**What you may do yourself.** A pilot (except a sport pilot) may do preventive maintenance on an airplane they own or operate that isn't used under parts 121, 129 or 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. With at least a private pilot certificate you may then approve it for return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]. Your entry needs the work done, the date, and your name, signature, certificate number and type [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

callout.text: Preventive maintenance is limited to the items in 14 CFR part 43, appendix A(c) [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Avionics and instrument repairs are for a mechanic or repair station. Report them; don't fix them.

check.q: A mechanic replaces your vacuum pump. What must exist before you fly the airplane?
check.a: Approval for return to service by an authorized person and the 43.9 maintenance record entry [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

chunks.title: Inoperative equipment after the flight: 91.213 and AC 91-67A

body.p: When you find an inoperative item, the choice is to cancel, get maintenance before flight, or defer it [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. There are two legal ways to defer: an approved MEL, or 91.213(d) [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

head: With an MEL
Without an MEL: 91.213(d)
rows: Paperwork
Approved MEL plus a letter of authorization in the airplane [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]
No application or approval needed [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]]
Who may use it
Once an LOA is issued, the MEL is mandatory for that airplane [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]
Small non-turbine airplanes and others in 91.213(d)(1); not turbine-powered airplanes [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2]]
Records
Entry describing the inoperable items in the records available to the pilot [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)(4)]]
43.9 entry for removal or for deactivation [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2]]

body.p: **What can't be deferred under 91.213(d).** The item may not be [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]:

bullets: Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment.
Required on the airplane's equipment list or on the KOEL for the kind of flight you're doing.
Required by 91.205 or another part 91 rule for that kind of flight.
Required to be operational by an airworthiness directive.

body.p: So for an IFR flight, nothing on the 91.205(d) list can be deferred: two-way radio and nav suitable for the route, turn rate indicator, slip-skid indicator, sensitive altimeter, clock with seconds, adequate generator or alternator, attitude indicator and heading indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. A KOEL item required for IFR can't be deferred for IFR either [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]].
**If it can be deferred, then all of these** [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]]:

bullets: Removed, with the cockpit control placarded and the work recorded per 43.9, or deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative'.
Removal or deactivation is done by a person authorized under 43.3, and that person makes the 43.9 entry. No one may fly the airplane without it [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.2]] [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].
Deactivation may take more than a switch off, such as pulling and securing a circuit breaker [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].
A rated pilot or mechanic decides the item is not a hazard to the aircraft [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

body.p: The placard goes next to the control or indicator, must be legible and visible, and must not hide other controls [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]]. The owner must have the item repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].

callout.text: Items that may not be deferred (PHAK examples: tachometer, flaps, stall warning) must be repaired before departure. If parts or maintenance aren't available, a special flight permit from the FSDO can let you fly it to a repair shop [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

body.p: In the next game, assume each item is not on the VFR-day type certification list, the equipment list or the KOEL unless the clue says otherwise.

check.q: Is an INOPERATIVE sticker alone enough to defer a broken item under 91.213(d)?
check.a: No. It must also not be required, be removed or deactivated with the 43.9 entry, and be found not to be a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]] [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

body.p: To use VOR under IFR, the VOR must be maintained under an approved procedure or operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and found within limits [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

head: Check
How
Max error
rows: VOT or repair station test signal
At the departure airport. CDI centered: OBS 0° FROM or 180° TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]
Ground checkpoint
Designated point on the airport surface [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(2)]]
Airborne checkpoint
Designated airborne checkpoint [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]]
Airway ground point
Prominent point on a VOR airway centerline, preferably more than 20 NM from the VOR, at a reasonably low altitude [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)]]
Dual VOR
Both receivers on the same VOR; compare bearings [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]
4° between them

body.p: A ground checkpoint is a painted circle with an arrow in the middle, aligned with the checkpoint azimuth, plus a black-on-yellow sign giving the VOR, the check course and DME [[33:156|AIM 2-3-6]] [[33:157|AIM 2-3-6]]. The circle has a white outer ring and a yellow ring, a yellow arrow aligned toward the facility, and a black interior on concrete [[33:160|AIM FIG 2-3-20]]. Locations are in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

callout.text: Yearly calibration by an authorized repair facility is recommended. A worn receiver can look fine close to the VOR or VOT and still be out of tolerance farther away [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

check.q: Which VOR check methods allow ±6° instead of ±4°?
check.a: The airborne checkpoint and the airway ground-point check [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)]].

chunks.title: Logging the VOR check and other IFR records

callout.text: Log it: the person making the check enters the date, place and bearing error, and signs the aircraft log or other record. If a repair station test signal is used, the repair station enters the bearing it transmitted and the date [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

body.p: If the check is out of tolerance, IFR flight must not be attempted until the error is corrected [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]. Write it up. Apply no correction except the manufacturer's correction card figures [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].
While you're in the records, note when other IFR checks expire: altimeter, static system and encoder (24 calendar months) and transponder (24 calendar months) [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].

check.q: You and a friend do a dual VOR check: 093° and 098°. Can you use VOR for IFR?
check.a: No. 5° is more than the 4° allowed [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. Log the result and write it up.

chunks.title: Risk: don't hand the next pilot your problem

body.p: Inoperative equipment is an "A" (aircraft) hazard in the PAVE checklist. Judge it against the expected conditions [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. A landing light isn't required for part 91 flights not for hire, but losing it still makes a night flight more hazardous [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

The RMH tells of a pilot whose vacuum pump failed in VMC, leaving the attitude indicator and directional gyro inoperative. Instead of diverting, the pilot continued into IMC, adding a "V" hazard to the "A" hazard [[30:11|RMH 1-2]].

head: Hazard
Mitigation
rows: Problem not recorded; next pilot doesn't know
Postflight inspection and a clear write-up identify hazards before the next person flies [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]
Repairs put off
Repair at the earliest opportunity to get back to the design level of safety [[58:8|AC 91-67A 1.7.4]]
Several small items inoperative together
Consider their combined effect and the extra workload [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]
Flying a deferred item into weather or night
Weigh adverse weather, night, airports, en route environment, alternates, workload and fatigue [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]
Unsecured airplane
Proper securing may prevent damage that could affect the next flight [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]

callout.text: Found it, write it. If you flew with it, someone else will too, unless the record says so.

body.p: Addressing discrepancies and doing proper maintenance increase reliability and reduce risk. So do thorough preflight and postflight inspections [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

check.q: Your landing light failed on a day VFR flight. It isn't required for your day flight tomorrow. Do you still write it up?
check.a: Yes. It is an "A" hazard to judge against expected conditions, and the next pilot may fly at night [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]; record it in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

bullets: Skipping the postflight walkaround because the flight went well [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
Telling ATC about a malfunction but never writing it up for maintenance [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
Vague squawks with no time, conditions or duration [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].
Blaming the VOR before trying a small rpm change [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].
Putting an INOP sticker on an item without the deactivation, 43.9 entry and hazard determination [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].
Deferring an item that 91.205(d), the KOEL or an AD requires for the flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]].
Doing a VOR check and not logging date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].
A pilot attempting repairs beyond preventive maintenance [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
Forgetting servicing: oil to POH level and fuel for the next use [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

check.q: What four things must a VOR check log entry show?
check.a: Date, place, bearing error and the signature of the person who did it [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

scenario.title: Low suction in the clouds and a club airplane booked for tomorrow
scenario.setup: You are flying a flying club's single-engine airplane on an IFR flight plan in IMC, in controlled airspace. The suction gauge drops below the green arc and the attitude indicator starts to tilt slowly. You use the POH procedure, go to partial panel, and land at your destination. On the ramp a dual VOR check you did en route sits in your notes: VOR 1 read 212°, VOR 2 read 218°. The oil is a quart low. Another member has the airplane booked for an IFR flight tomorrow morning and texts you: 'Just stick an INOP label on it and I'll go VFR if I have to.'

questions.q: When the suction dropped, what did you owe ATC, and what goes in the report?
questions.a: Report the malfunction as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]]. Include aircraft ID, equipment affected, how much your IFR capability is impaired, and the help you want [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]]. The AIM also asks for reports of other equipment that affects safety or IFR capability [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

questions.q: After shutdown, what do you inspect and document?
questions.a: Do the walkaround: cowling, tank areas, gear, brakes, inlets [[24:60|AFH 2-23]], plus antennas and pitot-static ports [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]. Write up the suction loss and attitude indicator with time, altitude and conditions, the VOR split, and the low oil, in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Bring the oil to the POH level [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

questions.q: Can the VORs be used for tomorrow's IFR flight?
questions.a: Not until the error is fixed. A dual check allows only 4° between receivers; yours showed 6° [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. Log the date, place and bearing error and sign it [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

questions.q: Can tomorrow's flight go IFR with the vacuum system inoperative?
questions.a: No. The attitude indicator and heading indicator are required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], and an item required by 91.205 for the flight may not be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

questions.q: What is wrong with 'just stick an INOP label on it' for a VFR flight?
questions.a: A placard alone is not a deferral. The item must not be required (type certification, equipment list or KOEL, 91.205, ADs), must be removed or deactivated by an authorized person who makes the 43.9 entry, and a rated pilot or mechanic must find it not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]] [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. The club's owner must also get it repaired [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]].

questions.q: A mechanic replaces the vacuum pump. What must be in the records before anyone flies?
questions.a: A 43.9 entry with the work, date and the approving person's signature, certificate number and kind of certificate [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]], and approval for return to service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

skills.do: Conduct a postflight inspection and document discrepancies and servicing requirements, if any (ACS IR.VIII.A.S1). The examiner watches you do the walkaround and may ask you to write up a simulated failure and say whether the airplane can go IFR next.
skills.practice: After every training flight, do the AFH 2-23 walkaround [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] plus the IFH antenna and pitot-static items [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]. Write any squawk on the school's discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], and walk through the 91.213(d) questions for one item each time [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

quiz.q: Under IFR in controlled airspace, when must you report a nav or comm malfunction to ATC?
options: As soon as practical
Only if you declare an emergency
Within 10 days, in writing
Only after landing, by telephone
quiz.why: The PIC must report in-flight malfunctions of navigation, approach or communication equipment to ATC as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]].

quiz.q: Your alternator fails in flight. According to the PHAK, how do you handle it during the flight?
options: Defer it under 91.213(d) and continue
Placard the alternator switch INOPERATIVE
Use the AFM/POH procedures
Look it up in the MEL before acting
quiz.why: Maintenance deferrals are not used for inflight discrepancies; the manufacturer's AFM/POH procedures are [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

quiz.q: Which IFR-specific items does the IFH add to the walkaround?
options: Tire pressure and brake pad thickness
Antennas, pitot tube and static ports
Seat rails and door latches
Propeller nicks and spinner
quiz.why: The IFH instrument system check starts with the condition of all antennas and the pitot tube and static ports [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

quiz.q: Which is NOT required in a 14 CFR 43.9 maintenance record entry?
options: Description of the work performed
Date the work was completed
Signature and certificate number of the approver
Aircraft total time in service
quiz.why: 43.9(a) requires description, date, name of the person doing the work, and the approver's signature, certificate number and kind [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. Total time in service is part of a 43.11 inspection entry [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)]].

quiz.q: Under AC 91-67A, who must make the 43.9 entry after an inoperative system is deactivated?
options: Any pilot who flies the airplane next
A person authorized to approve return to service under 43.7
The FSDO that issued the LOA
Nobody; deactivation needs no entry
quiz.why: Deactivation is not preventive maintenance; a person authorized under 43.7 must make the 43.9 entry, and no one may operate the aircraft without it [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

quiz.q: Your airplane's KOEL lists an item as required for IFR, and it is inoperative. For an IFR flight you may:
options: Defer it under 91.213(d) with a placard
Fly if a mechanic says it is not a hazard
Not defer it for that IFR flight
Fly if you report it to ATC first
quiz.why: Inoperative equipment required by the KOEL for a kind of operation may not be deferred for that operation [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)]].

quiz.q: An item was legally deferred and placarded under 91.213(d). When must the owner have it repaired, replaced, removed or inspected?
options: Within 10 flight hours
At the next required inspection
Within 30 days
Before the next IFR flight only
quiz.why: The owner or operator must have it repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].

quiz.q: Using a VOT with the CDI centered, what should the OBS read?
options: 0° with a FROM indication
0° with a TO indication
180° with a FROM indication
The VOT's published radial
quiz.why: With the CDI centered, the OBS should read 0° FROM or 180° TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]].

quiz.q: Per the RMH, what is one benefit of a postflight inspection?
options: It replaces the next pilot's preflight
It satisfies the 100-hour inspection
It can find hazards before the next person flies
It approves the airplane for return to service
quiz.why: Inspecting the aircraft after a flight may identify aircraft hazards before the next person flies it [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

takeaways: A flight ends when the airplane is secured and the discrepancies are written up.
In flight: AFM/POH procedures, and under IFR report nav, approach or comm failures to ATC (ID, equipment, impairment, help wanted).
Postflight: AFH walkaround plus antennas, pitot-static ports and fluids; service oil and fuel; secure the airplane.
Write squawks with what, when, how long and conditions in the discrepancy record.
91.213(d): not required by type cert, equipment list/KOEL, 91.205 or an AD; removed or deactivated with a 43.9 entry by an authorized person; placarded; found not a hazard.
VOR check within 30 days: ±4° ground, ±6° airborne, 4° dual. Log date, place, bearing error, signature.
Don't let the next pilot inherit your problem.
cfi_notes: Sources differ on deactivation. PHAK 9-10 says deactivation 'may be as simple as the pilot positioning a circuit breaker to the OFF position.' AC 91-67A (2023) 4.2.2 says deactivation is not preventive maintenance and an appropriately authorized person must do it and make the 43.9 entry. The lesson teaches the AC; expect examiners to probe this.

IFH 9-16 says the VOR check needs 'an appropriate endorsement' within 30 days and refers to the A/FD. 14 CFR 91.171(d) requires a log or record entry (date, place, bearing error, signature), not an endorsement, and checkpoint locations are now in the Chart Supplement (AIM 1-1-4).
Students confuse placarding with deferral. Have them recite all four parts of 91.213(d) for a real item on your airplane, using its equipment list and KOEL.

Make the student explain why 'maintenance deferrals are not used for inflight discrepancies' (PHAK 9-9): in flight you follow the POH; the deferral decision is made on the ground before the next takeoff.
Use the school's real squawk sheet. Grade write-ups on whether a mechanic could reproduce the problem from them.
Examiners commonly ask where the VOR check is logged and what you'd do with an inoperative item found on the postflight, including whether the airplane can still go IFR.
Point out that a 91.187 report helps finish this flight; only the discrepancy record reaches the next pilot.
gaps: No source gives a standard format for a squawk sheet or discrepancy record; teach the school's or owner's system.
Airplane-specific postflight items, suction ranges, oil levels, the equipment list and the KOEL come from the POH/AFM.
AC 91-67A Figure 4-1 (PIC Decision Sequence) is a graphic that is not readable in the uploaded text; the lesson teaches the sequence from the 91.213(d) and AC 91-67A text.
Postflight checks for electronic flight displays and their backup batteries are not detailed; the IFH says to use the flight manual procedures.
Operator MEL (M) and (O) procedures and the procedures document are not covered in detail here.

activities.title: True or false: noticing and reporting
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Under IFR in controlled airspace, a partial loss of ILS receiver capability should be reported to ATC.
cards.why: Yes. Complete or partial loss of ILS receiver capability is on the AIM list of reports [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

cards.s: If you told ATC about a failure, you don't need to write it up after landing.
cards.why: No. ATC gets the report for this flight [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]; maintenance needs an entry in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

cards.s: Some propeller rpm settings can make the VOR CDI swing as much as ±6°.
cards.why: Yes. A slight rpm change usually smooths it; check before reporting the VOR or your equipment [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

cards.s: An altimeter that reads 50 ft off field elevation with the current setting should be referred to a repair station.
cards.why: No. The IFH limit is 75 ft; beyond that the accuracy is questionable [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

cards.s: GPS problems should also be reported after the flight on the FAA GPS Anomaly Reporting Form.
cards.why: Yes, in addition to the initial report by radio or telephone [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]].

cards.s: You may defer an inflight failure under 91.213(d) while still airborne and keep going.
cards.why: No. Deferrals are not used for inflight discrepancies; use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

activities.title: Postflight in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Run the shutdown checklist, including the magneto grounding check
Walk around: streaks, stains, tires, brakes, inlets, antennas
Service oil and fuel for the next use
Tie down or hangar, with control locks and covers on

activities.title: Which record or report?
activities.intro: Tap an entry or report, then what it must contain.

pairs.r: ID, equipment, impairment, and help wanted from ATC
Work done, date, approver's signature, certificate number and kind
Type of inspection, date and aircraft total time
Signed, dated list to the owner; deferrable items placarded
Pilot with at least a private certificate signs it
Discrepancy record: what, when, how long, conditions

activities.title: No MEL: may it be deferred, or fix it first?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Must be fixed before this flight

items.t: Clock with seconds inoperative, IFR flight planned
Position lights inoperative, daytime VFR flight
Landing light out, day VFR, not for hire
Slip-skid indicator stuck, IFR flight planned
An airworthiness directive requires the item to work

activities.title: Name the parts of a VOR ground checkpoint
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.title: VOR and altimeter checks by the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: VOT on the ramp. With the CDI centered, the OBS reads 357° with a FROM flag. What is the bearing error, in degrees?
Over an airborne checkpoint published as the 245° radial, your VOR shows 251°. What is the bearing error, in degrees?
items.why: 251 - 245 = 6°. That is exactly the ±6° airborne limit, so it passes [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]].

items.q: Dual VOR check: VOR 1 shows 047° and VOR 2 shows 052° to the same station. How many degrees apart are they?
items.why: 052 - 047 = 5°. The limit is 4°, so this fails [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

items.q: Your last logged VOR check was September 28. Today is October 20. How many days ago was the check?
items.why: 2 days left in September (29, 30) plus 20 in October = 22 days, within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]].

items.q: Field elevation is 620 ft. With the current setting the altimeter reads 705 ft. How many feet is it off?
items.why: 705 - 620 = 85 ft. More than 75 ft makes its accuracy questionable; refer it to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

activities.title: A flickering VOR and tomorrow's lesson
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, the school's airplane, IFR in IMC in controlled airspace. The school has no MEL. Another student has the airplane booked for an IFR lesson tomorrow.

steps.s: Cruising at 6,000 ft, the VOR 1 CDI starts swinging about 5° either side. The flag stays out of view. What do you try first?
options: Report the VOR station out of service
A small change in propeller rpm
Declare an emergency
Turn VOR 1 off for the rest of the flight
steps.why: Some rpm settings make the CDI swing up to ±6°; a slight rpm change usually smooths it. Check this before reporting [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

steps.s: The rpm change doesn't help, and now the VOR 1 flag stays in view. You still have VOR 2 and an IFR GPS. What now?
options: Report it to ATC: ID, equipment, impairment, help wanted
Say nothing, since you still have GPS
Wait and phone the tower after landing
Squawk 7600
steps.why: Under IFR in controlled airspace, report nav malfunctions to ATC as soon as practical, with those four items [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

steps.s: You land and shut down. What do you do before you leave the airplane?
options: Leave it for the mechanic to discover
Pull the VOR 1 circuit breaker and go
Walk around, service, secure, and write up VOR 1 with time, altitude and what you saw
Text the next student and skip the record
steps.why: Do the postflight inspection and servicing [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] and record the discrepancy in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], with the details the AIM asks for [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].

steps.s: The dispatcher says: 'Just stick an INOP label on VOR 1 so the lesson can go.' Your best answer?
options: Fine, a placard is all 91.213(d) needs
Only if it isn't required, an authorized person deactivates it with a 43.9 entry, it's placarded, and it's found not a hazard
You'll remove the radio yourself tonight
Cross out the last VOR check entry instead
steps.why: 91.213(d) needs all of these [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]; deactivation and its 43.9 entry are done by an authorized person [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

steps.s: The shop repairs VOR 1 and signs it off. Before the next IFR flight you do a dual VOR check: 090° and 093°. What do you do?
options: Log the date, place, 3° error, and sign
Nothing; repaired radios need no check
Fail it; dual checks allow only 2°
Ask ATC to confirm the radial instead
steps.why: 3° is within the 4° dual limit [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]; enter date, place, bearing error and sign [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

final_quiz.q: On the ramp you tune the VOT. With the CDI centered, the OBS reads 356° with a FROM indication. What is the result?
options: Fail: the error is 6°
Fail: VOT checks must show TO
Pass, but only for VFR
Pass: the error is 4°, within ±4°
final_quiz.why: It should read 0° FROM [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]], so the error is 4°. The VOT limit is ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Over a designated airborne checkpoint published as the 113° radial, your VOR shows 120°. What do you do?
options: Use the VOR; airborne checks allow ±8°
Don't use the VOR for IFR; write it up
Use it and apply a 7° correction
Use it; only ground checks have limits
final_quiz.why: The error is 7°; the airborne limit is ±6° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]]. Don't attempt IFR until it's corrected, and apply no correction but the manufacturer's card [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your last logged VOR check was September 12. Can you use the VOR for an IFR flight on October 15?
options: Yes, the check is good for one calendar month
Yes, it is good until the end of October
No, it was 33 days ago; check it again first
No, VOR checks must be done on the day of flight
final_quiz.why: The check must be within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]]. September 12 to October 12 is 30 days, so October 15 is 33 days.

final_quiz.q: Field elevation is 1,135 ft. With the current altimeter setting, the altimeter reads 1,230 ft on the ramp and the same in the run-up area. What does the IFH say?
options: The accuracy is questionable; refer it to a repair station
Normal; up to 100 ft is acceptable
Reset the altimeter to read field elevation and fly IFR
Normal; ramp and field elevations always differ
final_quiz.why: The error is 95 ft. More than 75 ft makes accuracy questionable; refer it to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

final_quiz.q: Your filed TAS is 140 knots. After an equipment problem you can only cruise at 128 knots TAS. Must you tell ATC?
options: No, only changes of 15 percent are reported
No, TAS changes are never reported
Yes, but only if you are not in radar contact
Yes, it changed by more than 10 knots
final_quiz.why: Report a change of 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater, from the filed TAS [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]. 5 percent of 140 is 7, so 10 knots applies; 12 knots is more.

final_quiz.q: The position lights fail on your postflight. Tomorrow's flight is day VFR and there is no MEL. Which plan is legal?
options: Put an INOP sticker on the switch and go
Have an authorized person deactivate them with a 43.9 entry, placard, and judge them not a hazard
Write it up; no further action is needed for day flight
Get an LOA from the FSDO before the flight
final_quiz.why: If not required for the flight, the item must be deactivated or removed and placarded, with a determination it's not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]; the authorized person makes the 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

final_quiz.q: Your club received an LOA and an MEL for its airplane. An item is inoperative. Which rule do you use?
options: Either the MEL or 91.213(d), your choice
91.213(d), because it's simpler
The MEL; it becomes mandatory once the LOA is issued
Neither; any inoperative item grounds the airplane
final_quiz.why: Once an operator gets an MEL and LOA, use of the MEL becomes mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: A friend's single-engine turboprop has an inoperative cabin light and no MEL. Can it be deferred under 91.213(d)?
options: No, turbine-powered airplanes can't use 91.213(d)
Yes, all single-engine airplanes are eligible
Yes, if a pilot placards it
Yes, but only for VFR flights
final_quiz.why: Turbine-powered airplanes may not be operated under 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: You own your airplane and hold a private pilot certificate. You change the oil, which is preventive maintenance. What is required?
options: A mechanic must sign it off
Nothing; owners need no entry
Only a note on the squawk sheet
Your own entry: work, date, name, signature, certificate number and type
final_quiz.why: A pilot may do preventive maintenance on an aircraft they own or operate [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] and approve it for return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], with the entry the PHAK lists [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: At the annual, the mechanic finds an inoperative item that 91.213(d)(2) allows to stay inoperative. What must the mechanic do?
options: Nothing until the owner asks
Give the owner a signed, dated discrepancy list and placard the item
Ground the airplane until it's fixed
Report it to the FAA on Form 337
final_quiz.why: The inspector gives the owner a signed and dated list and placards each such item 'Inoperative' [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Away from home, the stall warning fails. It isn't deferrable for your airplane and no mechanic or parts are available. What is your legal option to get home for repair?
options: Defer it under 91.213(d) anyway
Fly it if you avoid slow flight
Get a special flight permit from the FSDO
Fly it if another pilot agrees it is safe
final_quiz.why: Items that aren't deferrable must be repaired before departure; if that isn't possible, a special flight permit lets you fly it to a repair location [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

final_quiz.q: Under IFR you see GPS position errors outside any NOTAMed test area. How should you report it?
options: Only in the aircraft discrepancy record
By radio to ATC now, then on the GPS Anomaly Reporting Form after landing
Only to the avionics shop at the next annual
No report is needed if RAIM gave no alert
final_quiz.why: Report to the controlling ATC facility right away, and report GPS problems postflight on the FAA form [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. GPS anomalies are on the AIM 5-3-3 list [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your VOR needle swings about ±5° in cruise. Before writing up the receiver or reporting the station, what should you try?
options: A small change in propeller rpm
Turning the nav radio off and on twice
Applying a 5° correction to the OBS
Climbing at least 1,000 ft
final_quiz.why: Some rpm settings cause CDI swings up to ±6°; a slight rpm change usually smooths it. Check this before reporting [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

final_quiz.q: Which inoperative item would stop tomorrow's IFR flight but is not on the 91.205 list for day VFR?
options: Airspeed indicator
Fuel gauge
Magnetic compass
Clock with a sweep-second pointer or digital display
final_quiz.why: The clock is added for IFR by 91.205(d)(6) [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. Airspeed, fuel gauges and the compass are day VFR items under 91.205(b), which IFR also needs.
